nodes.body:
1990 Jan 1. T. Duane Phillips; Mote Marine Laboratory
Note: Author and date assigned based on when SLHs were written at Mote.
FLELMR Code: 1728

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Spot
Scientific Name:  Leiostomus xanthurus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Osteichthyes
	Order: 	Perciformes
	Family: Sciaenidae

Other Common Names: Flat croaker, yellowtail; golden croaker during spawning season (327); goody, roach, and post croaker (47).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Most of the commercial food fish harvest of spot comes from the Chesapeake Bay and South Atlantic.  Contributes to the commercial bottom fish industry of Louisiana and Mississippi which uses it for fish meal and oil as well as pet food (269).  Taken primarily by otter trawl, but also by gill nets, haul seines, and pound nets (463).

Recreational:  Some recreational fishing for spot occurs on the Atlantic coast because they take bait readily and can be caught near bridges, piers, and wharves (269).  Fishery information for the Gulf of Mexico showed a total catch of 161,000 spot in 1988 (513).

Indicator:  This species is a bottom feeder which often accumulates contaminants and is a target species for the National Status and Trends Program (681).  It been tested for many pesticides, herbicides, heavy metals, and chlorination byproducts (269 463).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Spot range from the Gulf of Maine to the Bay of Campeche, Mexico in all depths to at least 205 m (112 fm).

Within Study Area:  A very common bay and Gulf species (327).  Common throughout the Indian River Lagoon, but higher abundances occur  in the northern end of the lagoon (1009).

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Migrations
nodes.body: Adults migrate seasonally between estuarine and coastal waters.  They enter bays and sounds in spring and move offshore in fall and winter to spawn (312 543 313 255 169 374 553 223) and avoid cold temperatures (116 350).  There is some evidence that they may not return after spawning and possibly die (543).  Larvae are probably carried by longshore currents or by direct across-shelf transport into nearshore waters, and into estuarine areas by tidal flow (150 463), then juveniles move up into low salinity headwater areas.  Juveniles begin to enter the estuaries at about 4 months (Joseph 1972).  They may ascend brackish water to fresh water during the spring and summer (313).  Older fish seem to prefer deeper water (506).  Some adults may not migrate back to inshore waters, but remain in deep waters (30_50 fathoms) in the Gulf (553).  Emigrate from estuaries at ca. 60 (730) to 88 mm TL (378 751).

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body: Eggs and early larvae are planktonic and pelagic, larvae are transported inshore into estuarine nursery areas where postlarval and juvenile spot are found.  Larvae are found at all depths.  Juveniles are often found in the shallow head waters of tidal creeks and are primarily benthic feeders.  Juveniles have been collected from the Loxahatchee River (264 887).  Adults migrate seasonally between estuarine and coastal waters and move offshore in fall.  Can live up to four years although the majority live only 2-3 years (363 269).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type:  Marine pelagic to riverine demersal or estuarine demersal depending on life stage.  Cowan and Shaw (150) collected larvae in the northern Gulf of Mexico on the continental shelf up to the 40 m isobath, or 130 km offshore.

Substrate:  Adults taken most frequently over mud and sand bottoms in inside waters and offshore waters to at least 132 m (169 498 350).  Also found over mud, sand, and sand shell bottom.  Juveniles found primarily in nursery areas with mud and detrital bottoms and are sometimes found in seagrass beds (463).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Salinity:  Spot is a euryhaline species.  Laboratory spawned eggs have developed at 30 - 35 ppt (Powell and Gordy 1980).  Cowan and Shaw (150) collected larvae from 26 to 36 ppt.  In another study, larvae <15 d were found only in waters above 19.3 C (in or near the Gulf Stream) and at 35 - 36 ppt.  They have been reared successfully in the laboratory at 30 - 35 ppt.  Juveniles have been found from 0 - 31 ppt, occurring in greater numbers at salinities above 10 ppt (374 751 561 47).  Adults seem to prefer a more polyhaline environment than juveniles.  Adults found from 0 - 60 ppt (313 725  Powell and Gordy 1980).

Temperature:  Spot tolerate temperatures from 1.2 - 36.7 C, however, extended periods of low temperatures have resulted in dead or stunned fish.  Death due to temperature is a function of size, acclimation and rapidity of temperature drop (47).  Young spot are more tolerant of cold than adults (47).  Juveniles have been collected at 4 to 35 C and larvae at 5 to 19.3 C (751 561 150 269).  The upper incipient lethal temperature for post larvae and small juvenile spot has been estimated at 35.2 C (463).  The critical thermal maximum for juvenile spot acclimated at 15 C was 31.0 C.

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  Sexual, diecious, oviparous, with external fertilization.
Mating/Spawning: Mating and spawning occur from late fall to early spring well offshore in moderately deep water (730 169 506 614 9 463) with possibly some activity near beaches and passes (543 498).  Spawning in the Gulf waters off Louisiana occur from near midshelf (ca. 65 km) out to 175 km from the coast (150).  In the northern Gulf, off Alabama probably from December to at least late February (506); in Louisiana waters from November through March (150); off Texas late November to April, peaks December to February (543 9); while Sheridan et al. (648) suggested a late fall peak, but no winter samples were taken.  Laboratory spawning occurred only at 17.5 - 25.0 C (269).

Fecundity: Fecundity ranges from 20,900 eggs in a 136 mm SL specimen to 514,400 eggs in a 178 mm SL specimen (648).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Eggs:  Sizes range from 0.72_0.87 mm (415 363).
Larvae/Juvenile:  Larvae hatch in about 48 h at 20 C at 1.6 - 1.7 mm SL transforming to juveniles at about 18 mm.  Larvae grow from 1.6 mm SL to 17 - 19 mm in 90 days.  Juveniles grow to 80 - 100 mm at ca. 7_35 mm/mo (611 415 363 758 Warlen and Chester 1985).
Adults:  Maturation occurs at the end of the second year or early in the third year on Atlantic coast.  In the Gulf of Mexico some spot mature at age I; males at 123 mm SL and females at 127 mm SL (648).  Can grow up to 1235 mm SL at a rate of ca. 50 - 60 mm SL/yr (363).  Short-lived species rarely attaining a maximum age of 5 years (463).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body:
Larval and postlarval: spot are planktivorous (463).  Postlarvae feed predominantly on copepods and larvae feed on zooplankton.
Juvenile: feed primarily on crustaceans, especially copepods, nematodes, and annelid worms (611).
Juveniles and adults: are opportunistic bottom feeders utilizing infaunal and epibenthic invertebrates (269).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Predation: Reported predators of spot include striped bass, weakfish, flounder, and silky shark (463).

sections.content:

FLELMR Code: 1728

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Common Name:  Spot
Scientific Name:  Leiostomus xanthurus

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Osteichthyes
	Order: 	Perciformes
	Family: Sciaenidae

Other Common Names: Flat croaker, yellowtail; golden croaker during spawning season (327); goody, roach, and post croaker (47).

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Most of the commercial food fish harvest of spot comes from the Chesapeake Bay and South Atlantic.  Contributes to the commercial bottom fish industry of Louisiana and Mississippi which uses it for fish meal and oil as well as pet food (269).  Taken primarily by otter trawl, but also by gill nets, haul seines, and pound nets (463).

Recreational:  Some recreational fishing for spot occurs on the Atlantic coast because they take bait readily and can be caught near bridges, piers, and wharves (269).  Fishery information for the Gulf of Mexico showed a total catch of 161,000 spot in 1988 (513).

Indicator:  This species is a bottom feeder which often accumulates contaminants and is a target species for the National Status and Trends Program (681).  It been tested for many pesticides, herbicides, heavy metals, and chlorination byproducts (269 463).

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Spot range from the Gulf of Maine to the Bay of Campeche, Mexico in all depths to at least 205 m (112 fm).

Within Study Area:  A very common bay and Gulf species (327).  Common throughout the Indian River Lagoon, but higher abundances occur  in the northern end of the lagoon (1009).

Mobility and Migration:

sections.heading: Migrations
sections.content: Adults migrate seasonally between estuarine and coastal waters.  They enter bays and sounds in spring and move offshore in fall and winter to spawn (312 543 313 255 169 374 553 223) and avoid cold temperatures (116 350).  There is some evidence that they may not return after spawning and possibly die (543).  Larvae are probably carried by longshore currents or by direct across-shelf transport into nearshore waters, and into estuarine areas by tidal flow (150 463), then juveniles move up into low salinity headwater areas.  Juveniles begin to enter the estuaries at about 4 months (Joseph 1972).  They may ascend brackish water to fresh water during the spring and summer (313).  Older fish seem to prefer deeper water (506).  Some adults may not migrate back to inshore waters, but remain in deep waters (30_50 fathoms) in the Gulf (553).  Emigrate from estuaries at ca. 60 (730) to 88 mm TL (378 751).

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content: Eggs and early larvae are planktonic and pelagic, larvae are transported inshore into estuarine nursery areas where postlarval and juvenile spot are found.  Larvae are found at all depths.  Juveniles are often found in the shallow head waters of tidal creeks and are primarily benthic feeders.  Juveniles have been collected from the Loxahatchee River (264 887).  Adults migrate seasonally between estuarine and coastal waters and move offshore in fall.  Can live up to four years although the majority live only 2-3 years (363 269).

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content:
Habitat Type:  Marine pelagic to riverine demersal or estuarine demersal depending on life stage.  Cowan and Shaw (150) collected larvae in the northern Gulf of Mexico on the continental shelf up to the 40 m isobath, or 130 km offshore.

Substrate:  Adults taken most frequently over mud and sand bottoms in inside waters and offshore waters to at least 132 m (169 498 350).  Also found over mud, sand, and sand shell bottom.  Juveniles found primarily in nursery areas with mud and detrital bottoms and are sometimes found in seagrass beds (463).

sections.heading: Physical/Chemical
sections.content:
Salinity:  Spot is a euryhaline species.  Laboratory spawned eggs have developed at 30 - 35 ppt (Powell and Gordy 1980).  Cowan and Shaw (150) collected larvae from 26 to 36 ppt.  In another study, larvae <15 d were found only in waters above 19.3 C (in or near the Gulf Stream) and at 35 - 36 ppt.  They have been reared successfully in the laboratory at 30 - 35 ppt.  Juveniles have been found from 0 - 31 ppt, occurring in greater numbers at salinities above 10 ppt (374 751 561 47).  Adults seem to prefer a more polyhaline environment than juveniles.  Adults found from 0 - 60 ppt (313 725  Powell and Gordy 1980).

Temperature:  Spot tolerate temperatures from 1.2 - 36.7 C, however, extended periods of low temperatures have resulted in dead or stunned fish.  Death due to temperature is a function of size, acclimation and rapidity of temperature drop (47).  Young spot are more tolerant of cold than adults (47).  Juveniles have been collected at 4 to 35 C and larvae at 5 to 19.3 C (751 561 150 269).  The upper incipient lethal temperature for post larvae and small juvenile spot has been estimated at 35.2 C (463).  The critical thermal maximum for juvenile spot acclimated at 15 C was 31.0 C.

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode:  Sexual, diecious, oviparous, with external fertilization.
Mating/Spawning: Mating and spawning occur from late fall to early spring well offshore in moderately deep water (730 169 506 614 9 463) with possibly some activity near beaches and passes (543 498).  Spawning in the Gulf waters off Louisiana occur from near midshelf (ca. 65 km) out to 175 km from the coast (150).  In the northern Gulf, off Alabama probably from December to at least late February (506); in Louisiana waters from November through March (150); off Texas late November to April, peaks December to February (543 9); while Sheridan et al. (648) suggested a late fall peak, but no winter samples were taken.  Laboratory spawning occurred only at 17.5 - 25.0 C (269).

Fecundity: Fecundity ranges from 20,900 eggs in a 136 mm SL specimen to 514,400 eggs in a 178 mm SL specimen (648).

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Eggs:  Sizes range from 0.72_0.87 mm (415 363).
Larvae/Juvenile:  Larvae hatch in about 48 h at 20 C at 1.6 - 1.7 mm SL transforming to juveniles at about 18 mm.  Larvae grow from 1.6 mm SL to 17 - 19 mm in 90 days.  Juveniles grow to 80 - 100 mm at ca. 7_35 mm/mo (611 415 363 758 Warlen and Chester 1985).
Adults:  Maturation occurs at the end of the second year or early in the third year on Atlantic coast.  In the Gulf of Mexico some spot mature at age I; males at 123 mm SL and females at 127 mm SL (648).  Can grow up to 1235 mm SL at a rate of ca. 50 - 60 mm SL/yr (363).  Short-lived species rarely attaining a maximum age of 5 years (463).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content:
Larval and postlarval: spot are planktivorous (463).  Postlarvae feed predominantly on copepods and larvae feed on zooplankton.
Juvenile: feed primarily on crustaceans, especially copepods, nematodes, and annelid worms (611).
Juveniles and adults: are opportunistic bottom feeders utilizing infaunal and epibenthic invertebrates (269).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content: Predation: Reported predators of spot include striped bass, weakfish, flounder, and silky shark (463).
